theory.intro: **Blood alcohol content (BAC)** measures the mass of alcohol in grams per $100\text{ mL}$ of blood. It depends on sex, body mass ($M\text{ kg}$), standard drinks consumed ($N$), and drinking time ($H\text{ hours}$).
facts: $\text{BAC}_{\text{male}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{6.8M}$, where $N$ is standard drinks, $H$ is hours, and $M$ is mass in kilograms.
$\text{BAC}_{\text{female}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{5.5M}$, where $5.5$ reflects a lower average body water content in females than males ($6.8$).

Each standard drink has $10\text{ g}$ of alcohol ($10N$). These formulas assume alcohol is metabolised at a fixed rate of $7.5\text{ g}$ per hour ($-7.5H$); this is a model assumption, not a universal biological rate.
Learner and provisional drivers must maintain a zero BAC ($0.00$), while unrestricted drivers must stay under $0.05$.
A negative formula result is nonphysical because BAC cannot be negative. It does not establish that a person's actual BAC is zero.
These formulas estimate BAC and omit factors including liver function, recent meals, physical fitness and individual differences.
steps: Select the male or female BAC formula
Substitute the values for drinks, hours, and mass
Evaluate or solve for the unknown quantity

workedExamples.question_text: A male weighing $84\text{ kg}$ consumes $5$ standard drinks over $2.5\text{ hours}$. Use $\text{BAC}_{\text{male}}=\dfrac{10N-7.5H}{6.8M}$ to calculate his estimated BAC, correct to 3 decimal places.

A female weighing $66\text{ kg}$ consumes $4$ standard drinks over $2.5\text{ hours}$. Use $\text{BAC}_{\text{female}}=\dfrac{10N-7.5H}{5.5M}$ to calculate her estimated BAC, correct to 3 decimal places.

A male weighing $88\text{ kg}$ consumes $N$ standard drinks over $4\text{ hours}$. Using $\text{BAC}_{\text{male}}=\dfrac{10N-7.5H}{6.8M}$, find $N$ when his estimated BAC is exactly $0.05$. Round to 2 decimal places.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}\text{BAC}_{\text{male}}&=\frac{10N-7.5H}{6.8M}\\0.05&=\frac{10N-7.5(4)}{6.8(88)}\\29.92&=10N-30\\59.92&=10N\\N&=5.992\\N&\approx5.99\end{aligned}$

The model gives approximately $5.99$ standard drinks.

workedExamples.question_text: A female weighing $70\text{ kg}$ consumes standard drinks over $4\text{ hours}$. Using $\text{BAC}_{\text{female}}=\dfrac{10N-7.5H}{5.5M}$, find the maximum whole number of standard drinks for which her estimated BAC is strictly below $0.05$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
First find the boundary where the estimated BAC equals $0.05$.

$\begin{aligned}0.05&=\frac{10N-7.5(4)}{5.5(70)}\\19.25&=10N-30\\49.25&=10N\\N&=4.925\end{aligned}$

For fixed mass and drinking time, estimated BAC increases as $N$ increases. Therefore $N<4.925$, so the maximum whole number is $4$ standard drinks.

A $100\text{ kg}$ male is drinking over a $6\text{-hour}$ period.
What is the maximum whole number of standard drinks he can consume so that his estimated BAC at the end of the period is strictly below $0.05$?
development.solution_text:
$\text{BAC}_{\text{male}} = \dfrac{10N - 7.5H}{6.8M}$
$0.05 = \dfrac{10N - 7.5(6)}{6.8(100)}$
$0.05 = \dfrac{10N - 45}{680}$
$34 = 10N - 45$
$10N = 79$
$N = 7.9$
The maximum whole number of drinks is $7$.
